summary: Surveys transport protocols designed to take less bandwidth, or add less delay, than standard TCP when sharing a bottleneck with it. Such lower-than-best-effort protocols suit delay-insensitive background traffic, like bulk transfers that should not slow down interactive use.

plainLanguage.summary: Some network traffic does not need to arrive quickly: a software update, a backup, a video being fetched for later. This memo reviews the ways people have tried to make that traffic take a smaller share of a busy link than ordinary TCP would take, and explains what each method watches to decide when to slow down.

questions: lower than best effort transport protocols
subtitle: Transport protocols designed to be polite to other traffic.

tldr.problem: Background transfers such as bulk downloads and software updates take more of a shared link than they need to, and slow down the interactive traffic sharing it.
tldr.mechanism: The document surveys protocols designed to yield to standard TCP on a shared bottleneck, grouped into delay-based methods, non-delay-based methods, upper-layer approaches and network-assisted approaches, and describes how each one decides to back off.
tldr.outcome: It is a survey rather than a specification. Its purpose is to put the LEDBAT algorithm, which its authors' working group had just specified, in the context of the other work, and to note where delay-based detection is unreliable.

facts.value: alpha and beta, with alpha less than beta

today: RFC 6297 is an Informational document from June 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It is a survey, not a specification, and it places the LEDBAT algorithm in the context of the other work described in it.

sections.title: What the Survey Covers and How It Groups the Work
sections.content:
The document presents a brief survey of proposals to attain a Less-than-Best-Effort service by means of end-host mechanisms. It loosely defines an LBE service as a service which results in smaller bandwidth and/or delay impact on standard TCP than standard TCP itself, when sharing a bottleneck with it. Systems designed to provide this service are called LBE systems. With the exception of TCP Vegas, which is presented for historical reasons, systems that have been noted to exhibit LBE behaviour under some circumstances but were not designed for the purpose are excluded.

Generally, LBE behaviour can be achieved by reacting to queue growth earlier than standard TCP would, or by changing the congestion-avoidance behaviour of TCP without using any additional implicit feedback. It is therefore assumed that readers are familiar with TCP congestion control (RFC 5681). Some mechanisms achieve LBE behaviour without modifying transport-protocol standards, for example by changing the receiver window of standard TCP, while others use network-level mechanisms at the transport layer. According to this classification, solutions are categorized in the document as delay-based transport protocols, non-delay-based transport protocols, upper-layer approaches and network-assisted approaches. Some of the schemes in the first two categories could be implemented using TCP without changing its header format, which would facilitate their deployment in the Internet. The schemes in the third category are, by design, supposed to be especially easy to deploy because they only describe a way in which existing transport protocols are used. Finally, mechanisms in the last category require changes to equipment along the path, which can greatly complicate their deployment.

The document is a product of the Low Extra Delay Background Transport working group. It aims at putting the congestion control algorithm that the working group has specified in the context of the state of the art in LBE transport. The survey is not exhaustive, as the authors note this would not be possible or useful, and they have selected key, well-known or otherwise interesting techniques for inclusion at their discretion. There is also work related to the LBE concept that does not present a solution installable in end hosts or expected to work over the Internet, such as a Diffserv-based Lower-Effort service (RFC 3662), and that work is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo groups the work into four families, and the grouping is really about where the change is made. Some methods change the transport protocol itself and watch the delay. Some change it and watch for lost packets instead. Some leave the protocol alone and change how the application behaves. And some need the routers to help.

sections.title: Delay-Based Transport Protocols
sections.content:
It is wrong to generally equate little impact on standard TCP with a small sending rate. Without Explicit Congestion Notification support, standard TCP will normally increase its congestion window and effective sending rate until a queue overflows, causing one or more packets to be dropped and the effective rate to be reduced. A protocol that stops increasing the rate before this event happens can, in principle, achieve a better performance than standard TCP.

TCP Vegas is one of the first protocols known to have a smaller sending rate than standard TCP when both share a bottleneck, yet it was designed to achieve more, not less, throughput than standard TCP. When TCP Vegas is the only congestion control algorithm used by flows going through the bottleneck, its throughput is greater than that of standard TCP, and depending on the bottleneck queue length it can itself be starved by standard TCP flows, which Random Early Detection can remedy to some degree. Vegas linearly increases or decreases the sending rate based on the difference between expected and actual throughput, estimated from RTT measurements. In congestion avoidance, once per RTT, Vegas calculates the expected throughput as WindowSize divided by BaseRTT, where WindowSize is the current congestion window and BaseRTT is the minimum of all measured RTTs, and compares it with the actual throughput measured from recent acknowledgements. If the actual throughput is smaller than the expected throughput minus a threshold called beta, that is taken as a sign of congestion and the rate is linearly decreased; if the actual throughput is greater than the expected throughput minus a threshold called alpha, with alpha less than beta, the network is taken to be underutilized and the rate is linearly increased.

TCP Nice follows the same basic approach as Vegas but removes the issue that Vegas's moderate linear decrease can still affect standard TCP: Nice halves the congestion window, at most once per RTT like standard TCP, instead of reducing it linearly, and only if a fixed predefined fraction of delay-based incipient congestion signals appears within one RTT. Otherwise TCP Nice falls back to the congestion-avoidance rules of Vegas if no packet was lost, or standard TCP if a packet was lost. It can also support a congestion window of less than one packet, by clocking out single packets over more than one RTT.

TCP Low Priority uses only the one-way delay instead of the RTT as an indicator of incipient congestion, to avoid reacting to delay fluctuations caused by reverse cross-traffic. Using the TCP Timestamps option, the one-way delay is determined as the difference between the receiver's timestamp value in the acknowledgement and the original timestamp value copied into it; the result can only represent the one-way delay precisely if clocks are synchronized, but its absolute value is of no concern to TCP-LP, so clock synchronization is unnecessary. Using a constant smoothing parameter, TCP-LP calculates an exponentially weighted moving average of the measured one-way delay and checks whether the result exceeds a threshold within the range of the minimum and maximum one-way delay seen during the connection's lifetime, which it interprets as an early congestion indication; the minimum and maximum values are initialised during slow start.

On reaction to an early congestion indication, TCP-LP strikes a middle ground between setting the congestion window to one packet immediately and halving it like standard TCP: it delays the former action by an additional RTT to see whether congestion persists. It halves the window at first, then starts an inference time-out timer and maintains the current window until the timer fires; if another early congestion indication appears during that inference phase, the window is set to one, otherwise it is maintained and the window continues to grow in the standard additive-increase fashion. This ensures it takes at least two RTTs for a TCP-LP flow to decrease its window to one, and that, like standard TCP, it reacts to congestion at most once per RTT. Sync-TCP adapts its reaction according to changes in the one-way delay, comparing the estimated average forward queuing delay with the maximum observed delay and adapting the AIMD parameters to the trend of the average delay over an observation window.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea in this family is to notice a queue forming before packets start being dropped. TCP Vegas compares the throughput it expects at the current window size with the throughput it actually gets, and a lower actual means the queue is growing. TCP Low Priority watches the delay in one direction only, so that traffic coming back the other way does not confuse it.

sections.title: How Well Does Delay Predict Congestion
sections.content:
The accuracy of delay-based congestion predictors has been the subject of a good deal of research. The main result of most of these studies is that delays, or more precisely round-trip times, are in general weakly correlated with congestion. Several factors may induce such a poor correlation.

The first is bottleneck buffer size: in principle a delay-based mechanism could be made more than TCP friendly if buffers are large enough, so that RTT fluctuations and deviations from the minimum RTT can be detected by the end host with reasonable accuracy. Otherwise it may be hard to distinguish real delay variations from measurement noise. The second is RTT measurement issues: samples may suffer from poor resolution, due to timers too coarse-grained with respect to the scale of delay fluctuations, and a flow may obtain a very noisy estimate of RTTs due to undersampling, for example when the flow rate is much lower than the link bandwidth. For TCP, other potential sources of measurement noise include TCP segmentation offloading and the use of delayed acknowledgements. A congested reverse path may also result in an erroneous assessment of the congestion state of the forward path, and in the case of fast or short-distance links the majority of the measured delay can be due to processing in the involved hosts, which typically is not of interest and can underlie fluctuations unrelated to the network.

The third is the level of statistical multiplexing and RTT sampling: it may be easy for an individual flow to miss loss or queue overflow events, especially if the number of flows sharing a bottleneck buffer is significant. The fourth is the impact of wireless links: mechanisms typical of wireless links, such as link-layer scheduling and error recovery, may induce strong delay fluctuations over short timescales.

Other results paint a slightly different picture. Bhandarkar and others claim it is possible to significantly improve prediction accuracy by adopting simple techniques such as smoothing of RTT samples and increasing the RTT sampling frequency. They acknowledge, however, that even with such techniques it is not possible to eradicate detection errors, and their proposed method, PERT, mitigates the impact of residual detection errors with a probabilistic response mechanism to congestion-detection events.

Whether a delay-based protocol behaves in its intended manner may depend on these accuracy issues. Protocols like Vegas need to keep an estimate of the minimum, that is the base, delay, which makes them highly sensitive to changes in the end-to-end route during the lifetime of the flow. On false positives and false negatives, most studies focus on the loss of throughput coming from erroneous detection of queue build-up and of alleviation of congestion. For an LBE transport protocol it is arguably better to err on the more-than-TCP-friendly side, that is, always to yield to perceived congestion whether it is real or not; failure to detect congestion, however, would result in behaviour that is not LBE. For instance, where the bottleneck buffer is small, so that the contribution of queuing delay at the bottleneck to the global end-to-end delay is small, a flow using a delay-based mechanism might end up consuming a good deal of bandwidth relative to a competing standard TCP flow, unless it also incorporates a suitable reaction to loss.

A delay-based mechanism may also suffer from the latecomer advantage problem. Where the bottleneck link is already very congested, delay variations may be quite small, so it may be very difficult to tell an empty queue from a heavily loaded one in terms of delay fluctuation. A newly arriving delay-based flow may therefore start sending faster when there is already heavy congestion, eventually driving away loss-based flows.
sections.plainLanguage: Delay is a weak signal, and the memo explains why: small buffers hide the queue, measurement noise hides it further, and a single flow among many may never see the overflow at all. The safer choice for a background protocol is to give way whenever it thinks there is congestion, even if it is wrong.

sections.title: Other Transport Protocols and Upper-Layer Approaches
sections.content:
A few transport-layer proposals achieve an LBE service without relying on delay as an indicator of congestion. In those algorithms the loss rate of the flow determines, implicitly or explicitly, the sending rate, which is adapted so as to obtain a lower share of the available bandwidth than standard TCP. Such mechanisms likely cause more queuing delay and react to congestion more slowly than delay-based ones.

4CP, which stands for Competitive and Considerate Congestion Control, provides an LBE service by changing the window control rules of standard TCP. A virtual window is maintained that, during a so-called bad congestion phase, is reduced to less than a predefined minimum value of the actual congestion window; the congestion window is only increased again once the virtual window exceeds this minimum, and in this way the virtual window controls the duration during which the sender transmits with a fixed minimum rate. Whether the congestion state is bad or good depends on whether the loss event rate is above or below a threshold value. The algorithm allows a target average window to be set and avoids the starvation of background flows while bounding the impact on foreground flows.

MulTFRC is an extension of TCP-Friendly Rate Control (RFC 5348) for multiple flows. A single MulTCP flow tries to emulate, and be as friendly as, a number N greater than one of parallel TCP flows. By supporting values of N between 0 and 1, MulTFRC can be used as a mechanism for an LBE service. Since it does not react to delay but adjusts its rate like TCP-Friendly Rate Control, it can probably be expected to be more aggressive than mechanisms such as TCP Nice or TCP Low Priority, which also means it is less likely to be prone to starvation, as its aggressiveness is tunable at a fine granularity even when N is between 0 and 1.

The upper-layer approaches do not require modifying transport-protocol standards. Most can be regarded as running on top of an existing transport, even though they may be implemented either at the application layer, in user-level processes, or in the kernel of the operating system. Such mechanisms may be easier to deploy, since they require no changes to the transport itself. A simplistic application-level approach may consist in scheduling automated transfers at times when the network is lightly loaded, but that may not be applicable to applications such as peer-to-peer file transfer, since the notion of an off-peak hour is not meaningful when end hosts may be located anywhere in the world. The Background Intelligent Transfer Service is implemented in several versions of Microsoft Windows and uses a system of application-layer priority levels for file-transfer jobs together with monitoring of bandwidth usage of the network interface, or in more recent versions of the network gateway, so that low-priority transfers at a given end host give way to both high-priority transfers and traffic from interactive applications at the same host. A different approach reduces the priority of a flow via a generic idletime scheduling strategy in the host's operating system, but it rests on the assumption that all involved end hosts would use the scheduler, so it does not protect a standard TCP flow originating from any host where the scheme is not implemented.

Some proposals exploit existing transport-layer features, typically at the receiving side: TCP's built-in flow control can be used as a means of achieving a low-priority transport service. One such mechanism controls the bandwidth by letting the receiver intelligently manipulate the receiver window of standard TCP, possible because the authors assume a client-server setting where the receiver's access link is typically the bottleneck. It incorporates a delay-based calculation of the expected queue length at the bottleneck, quite similar to the calculation in the delay-based protocols. Another method dynamically adapts both the advertised receiver window and the delay in sending acknowledgements to attain a given rate, and also proposes a bandwidth-sharing system that allocates bandwidth among flows and allots a minimum rate to some of them. Receiver window tuning is also done by choosing the right value for the window as an optimization problem, with a binary search algorithm that is faster but fluctuates and a stochastic optimization algorithm that does not fluctuate but converges more slowly.
sections.plainLanguage: Other designs give up on delay. Some watch for lost packets instead, which is slower to react but easier to get right. Some do not touch the transport at all: a background transfer service that pauses when the link is busy, or an operating system that gives low-priority tasks less of the machine.

sections.title: Network-Assisted Approaches
sections.content:
Network-layer mechanisms, such as active queue management and packet scheduling in routers, can be exploited by a transport protocol for achieving an LBE service. Such approaches may result in improved protection of non-LBE flows, for example when scheduling is used, and approaches using an explicit, active queue management based congestion signalling may arguably be more robust than delay-based transports for detecting impending congestion. The obvious drawback of any network-assisted approach is that, in principle, they need modifications in both end hosts and intermediate network nodes.

Harp realizes an LBE service by dissipating background traffic to less utilized paths of the network, based on multipath routing and multipath congestion control, achieved without changing all routers by using edge nodes as relays. It detects impending congestion by looking at delay, similar to TCP Nice, and improves the utilization and fairness of TCP over pure single-path solutions without requiring any changes to TCP itself.

Another technique is used by protocols like Network-Friendly TCP, where a bandwidth-estimation module integrated into the transport protocol allows the protocol to rapidly take advantage of free capacity. Network-Friendly TCP combines this with early congestion detection based on Explicit Congestion Notification (RFC 3168) and Random Early Detection (RFC 2309); when congestion starts building up, appropriate tuning of a Random Early Detection queue allows low-priority packets to be marked with a much higher probability than high-priority ones, so that low-priority flows yield up bandwidth before standard TCP flows. It could be implemented by adapting the congestion control behaviour of TCP without changing the protocol on the wire, with the only exception that capable routers must be able to distinguish its traffic from other TCP traffic.

Another approach leverages an existing network-layer LBE service based on priority queueing. The Priority-Layer Transport protocol splits a layer-4 connection into two flows, a high-priority one and a low-priority one. The high-priority flow is sent over the higher-priority queueing class, in principle offering a best-effort service, using an AIMD, TCP-like congestion control mechanism, while the low-priority flow, mapped to the LBE class, uses a non-TCP-friendly congestion control algorithm. The goal is to maximise aggregate throughput by exploiting unused capacity in an aggressive way while protecting standard TCP flows carried by the best-effort class. The receiver monitors the loss rate of both flows; if the high-priority flow starts seeing losses while the low-priority one does not experience total loss, that is taken as an indication of the absence of strict priority queueing, and the non-TCP-friendly flow may be inhibited.
sections.plainLanguage: The last family asks the network to help. Routers mark the low-priority packets, so the background flow gives way before ordinary TCP feels any pain. Or the routers queue one class of traffic ahead of another, and the transport splits its connection into two so it can use the cheap queue for bulk data. These need changes in the routers as well as the hosts.

sections.title: Where LEDBAT Sits and What the Survey Concludes
sections.content:
The previous sections show a large amount of work on attaining an LBE service, heterogeneous in nature. The algorithm developed by the LEDBAT working group can be classified as a delay-based mechanism; as such, it is similar in spirit to the protocols in the delay-based section. It is, however, not a protocol: how it is actually applied to the Internet, that is, how to use existing or even new transport protocols together with the LEDBAT algorithm, is not defined by the working group. As it heavily relies on delay, the discussion about the accuracy of delay-based detection and the issues with delay-based congestion control for LBE transport applies to it as well. The performance of LEDBAT has been analysed in comparison with some of the other work in several articles, but these analyses have to be examined with care, because at the time of writing LEDBAT was still a moving target.

The document introduces no new security considerations. It also notes that work related to the LBE concept that cannot be installed in end hosts or expected to work over the Internet, such as a Diffserv-based Lower-Effort service, lies outside its scope, along with the mechanism the IETF Congestion Exposure working group is developing which could incentivise LEDBAT-like applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm this working group wrote, LEDBAT, is in the delay-based family, so it inherits both the advantages and the weaknesses described earlier. It is not a complete protocol: it is the congestion control part, and how to combine it with a transport is still open. The memo concludes that the field is fragmented and that the delay-based methods rest on a signal that is not always reliable.

items.title: Delay-based transport
items.text: The transport watches the round trip or one-way delay and backs off before packets are lost.

items.title: Non-delay-based transport
items.text: The loss rate sets the sending rate, which reacts more slowly but does not depend on delay measurement.

items.title: Upper-layer approaches
items.text: The transport is untouched; the application or the operating system decides when to send and how much.

items.title: Network-assisted approaches
items.text: Routers mark or queue the background traffic, which needs changes along the path.

viz.caption: THE DELAY-BASED PROTOCOLS AND HOW EACH ONE BACKS OFF

cells: Compares expected and actual throughput and changes the rate linearly, using the alpha and beta thresholds
Halves the window instead of a linear decrease, but only if enough signals arrive within one RTT
Halves the window, then waits an extra RTT before cutting it to one packet
Adapts the AIMD parameters to the trend of the average delay over an observation window

viz.caption: WHY DELAY IS A WEAK SIGNAL OF CONGESTION

items.title: Buffer size
items.text: With small buffers the queue never builds up enough to show up in the round trip time.

items.title: Measurement noise
items.text: Coarse timers, delayed acknowledgements, segmentation offloading and host processing all distort the measurement.

items.title: Many flows sharing the buffer
items.text: A single flow may never see the overflow that the delay signal is supposed to reveal.

items.title: Wireless links
items.text: Link-layer scheduling and error recovery cause delay swings that have nothing to do with congestion.
